hits.author: subparsec
hits.title: Show HN: Built Taskman, a Rust TUI for Parallel Claude/Codex Work on Issues+PRs

story_text.value:
I'm a software engineer from the east coast (who has lived in Boston, NY, the bay area, UK, France), and I built a task system called 3 & Done. It's the place you trust to store everything you need to do. It accepts voice input for rapid entry, as well as text (it stores the audio locally so you can listen to jog your memory) and emails you every morning with the three most important things for you to do that day, and why, based on what you've said about the task: deadlines, urgency, sitting too long.

I've been at software engineering for about 44 years now... Grew up with it, which was unusual when I started, and I was always good about getting into the zone and doing things. The career started small, small company, then back office, the dot com startups, then smaller companies again after the bust, a non-profit, and eventually YouTube (Google at the time, but just barely) and Meta (just Facebook when I was there).

When I hit the startups, and later big tech, it was no longer enough to just be an engineer, to have drive, to be good, you had to be organized, you had to follow through, get stuff done, and that's where the task systems started. Twenty-five over the years (and yes, I've actually counted), from Moleskine notebooks with Getting Things Done, evernote (remember evernote?), bug trackers, todoist, asana, google keep, among others.

When I managed on the Facebook News Feed, I got into gantt charts (for me and my team), spreadsheets, OmniPlan... I remember apologizing to my director for being so disorganized (because I felt I was making a mess of it), and he told me that I was the most organized engineer he knew.

That was because I was doing all of the work in the background, the trimming, the sorting, the reviews, but it was just so much work. Which was why I changed from system to system. Each time it built up, and I had to spend more time looking at things I couldn't or didn't get done, when I was rushed and couldn't put time into today's review, it would pile up, and then using it was so much work that I would start taking mini-notes, just emailing myself a few things to do the next day.

That's actually the thesis of the app (but not where it started), that if I could just have a few things to do emailed to me each day, I could get it done.

This app actually started when I described my previous startup failures into a Claude web session, and it repeated back to me what I had just said. My previous failures were because I spent too much time building the stuff I needed, and not building what I was supposed to be building.

I decided that the app would email me three things to do every day (which matches best practices for attention), but that the day was always yours to decide. We won't overload you, but you can add more, if you're feeling up to it, or cut back, and we never shame and try our best not to nag (I often only finish two). If we get it wrong, you can tell us, and we'll re-rank it once a day, or you can set it manually, and if you do, we never override that choice. The web app is live, and native for both platforms is coming. In the meantime, on Android, you can use gestures to quick launch into the voice input so saving a task is only a gesture away (e.g. double-tap the back of a Pixel, double-press the power button on Motorola).

Now let's talk about the dirty parts. I used AI to help me build this. Anthropic models mostly, and the brains of the app come from Anthropic models (I like the quality, I like the privacy, absolutely no training on customer data, and the stance of the company). This app is not some one-shot wonder where I asked frontier models to build a task system and then I put it on a server to show you.

I have prompts for the various features (e.g. ranking, generating suggestions, task extractions), I have eval sets of task lists (not anyone's real tasks, but constructed from patterns in my tasks, or the tasks of testers who allowed me to fix the problems they were having), with the three I expect to come out. I store the eval outputs, and re-test whenever I add a new rule to a prompt, or whenever testing a new model version. The great thing about having this eval set is that it catches when I get it wrong. When I introspect a failed run, sometimes it's because I need to tune a prompt, but sometimes it's because I missed something in my own ranking.

I did the same thing with my infrastructure as well, so this time, instead of setting up servers, and building login systems, and managing databases, I built on Vercel (git push to serving Next.js), Neon (hosted postgres).

I started getting emails mailed to me by mid-June, but started getting usable suggestions on June 26, and I've been using it every morning since. I wanted it to be easy to get started, and easy to use, so the input handles mess (you can add multiple tasks in the same run-on sentence, and a friend who helped me test it just pasted his entire obsidian todo list in wholesale to get started).

I wanted to make sure that anyone could try it out, so I built a trial feature that uses the real in-app ranking with a list of items you provide.

If you want to try the service, there's a free 14-day trial (card required), and then it's $99/year or $9.99/month after that (plus sales tax). We warn you seven days before your card is charged and if you cancel, you keep access through the term (either the trial, or our last paid period). Online, through settings -> billing, no email, no call.

I really hope you'll try it out. If you do, please tell me if we did a good job picking out your day.

https://3anddoneapp.com/try

story_text.value:
Prathmesh, CEO of MCPJam here.

Users now start in ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and other AI clients. They reach your product through your MCP server.

That means your users often aren’t in your product anymore. You can’t see what they prompted for, how the agent interpreted it, or whether your server helped them get the result they wanted.

I saw this firsthand leading MCP technical strategy at Asana, including our ChatGPT and Claude launches. We were building high-stakes enterprise integrations, but we had no reliable way to test them the way we test normal software- or to know whether they worked once they reached real users.

I started using MCPJam for those problems after re-connecting with my former coworker who created the project. brought it to more of our developers, and worked it into our CI/CD pipeline. I joined the team because I kept hearing the same issue from other companies building for agents.

So, what does “good” look like for MCP? For us, it means users reliably get the outcome they came for, across the AI clients they use.

That’s what we’ve been building toward. MCPJam now helps you test the full workflow, from the first prompt to the expected result:

* Swarms: Simulate users with different goals and prompts to find where workflows break across AI clients. * User Testing: Watch how real users interact with your MCP product, where they get stuck, and how they feel about the results. * Evals: Turn those workflows into repeatable tests that check whether users get the expected outcome. * CI/CD: Run those evals across AI clients before each release to catch regressions.

Over 106,000 developers and +300 enterprises use our open-source solution to see how their servers behave locally across major AI clients. MCPJam has grown from a debugging tool into a continuous testing and evaluation workflow for MCP servers.

If you’re building an MCP server or agent-facing product, give MCPJam a try. What is the hardest thing for you to test? We love hearing about your MCP server builds!

story_text.value:
For the past few years i've been on Duolingo & was able to learn Hindi & Spanish (even helped me get state seal of biliteracy)

One of the biggest problems that I see in my generation (Gen Z) is loneliness. I love Duolingo's community, but sometimes (well actually oftentimes), I felt myself struggling to come back.

Online language learning is a skill where dominantly, the entire motivation is connection and the entire daily practice is solitude.

Nobody learns Spanish to know Spanish. They learn it to talk to their partner's family, to not be the silent one at the table, to move somewhere and have a life there. Then they spend 90 days alone with an owl.

I was thinking of a way to connect people around the globe-through the shared passion of learning languages, & creating a competitive social space where people could compete in rapid-fire matches, instantly get feedback, & learn through teaching their own avatar (vs a more passive "lesson-style" learning). They learn on the spot, under pressure, & are put in different situations where they have to maneuver through different absurd scenarios & speak or type the language in a satisfactory way).

The core flow is: Learn (2–5 min interactive segment) → Teach (explain it to your avatar) → Avatar attempts (your score).

Then you take that into ranked 1v1 matches against someone near your level, chess.com style: a blind judge grades both players on speaking and writing, ratings move, there's a global ladder with titles and perks.

The point is to bridge this through competition & internal community-building. Beyond the sport, users can interact with each other & create micro-societies based on their shared interests of the language. People learning Spanish who have gotten an interest in creating foods-stuff like Carne Asada or Gazpacho would join a community (based on their shared interest of the language).

On the technical side I found an interesting mix of problems (that turned out to just be one).

Matchmaking needs P(A beats B) from two ratings. Grading open-ended output is unreliable with rubrics, so instead of scoring one answer I only ever ask "which of these two is better", Comparative Judgment, with scores recovered via Bradley–Terry. Calibrating content difficulty across CEFR/JLPT levels is Item Response Theory, usually a Rasch model.

All three are the same logistic function. Elo is an online gradient step on the Bradley–Terry likelihood; Rasch is Bradley–Terry with one side fixed as "the item." So a 1v1 match is the pairwise comparison the judge needs, the judge's output is the observation the rating update consumes, and item difficulty falls out of the same fit. Ratings are Glicko-2, so a new player carries explicit uncertainty (high RD) and converges in a handful of matches instead of thirty. Users see it as a Fluency Score.

Two Questions: The human one: does competition make you want to practice, or does it just make you anxious about practicing?

If you've shipped LLM-as-judge somewhere the score had real consequences, how did you detect drift you couldn't see from inside the system?

If you think you may benefit/want to use from this, I put together a small waitlist of people who might be interested in using this in the future (I also put a small demo of a little creative writing prompt on the site... see if you can get highest accuracy!)

Thanks for taking the time to read https://thelingo.xyz

story_text.value:
I wanted a rotten tomatoes for ai film, hence popcorn.movie, because AI films need a critical and technical review that's different to movies, and we're in the 1895-1920's of ai movies right now.

Many festivals, people, industries, sites reject or suppress ai, for many great reasons (slop), and of course slopscrolling and other sites have the slop problem, as does this - the idea is to look past the slop to the real stories and technically great content, with an view that ai is a tool.

"is this stuff actually getting good, and which models are doing it?". Hot or slop.

My personal interest in ai video, probably stupid - try to actually visualize my dreams through prompts. I've tried it, but it never quite works, but it's fun.

--details

The site doesn't host video (everything plays via youtube-nocookie embeds). The product is the ranking, the many detailed breakdowns of voice sync, glitches, discussions.

If you love looking at coherence and how models are moving along, while seeing short and long form film content that is posted for ai festivals, check it out. Some of them have surprised me a lot. There's some 2 minute short films in here that are legit memorable and make you think, the stuff you imagine has been "let our of people's minds" by these tools.

- Every film records what it was made with (Seedance, Veo, Kling, Sora, mocap, Blender, real footage…), so there are per-tool leaderboards: which models produce watchable film (barren as heckfire right now, use the bookmarklet to add and review? get creators to share more about process)

- Votes only count toward the score if you actually watched a meaningful chunk (tracked via the IFrame API). Verdicts use a Wilson lower bound over reputation-weighted votes, star scores are Bayesian-shrunk toward the site mean, and voter reputation is a Beta distribution updated when a film's verdict settles. An openly pro-AI film site is a brigading magnet from both directions; the math is the defense.

- It tracks AI film festivals as they happen on YouTube i.e. Astana's #SpecialForAAIFF wave, Reply's Venice festival, Chroma, Project Odyssey, each with its verified submissions ranked.

- For the appreciation-society crowd there's a 46-axis breakdown (character consistency, temporal coherence, complex interaction; hands, eating, two bodies, generative necessity, je ne sais quoi). Every axis optional; unrated means not-applicable, not zero.

(I initially added a few to make it 42... then realized I needed more, ho hum)

--verbose details

Stack, for the curious: Go + Postgres + HTMX + Mustache, one binary, no SPA, no analytics vendor. Sign-in is Google, reviewers get generated olde-English pen names.

It's early, the catalogue is ~120 films seeded from festival hashtags and the voting community is tiny, so the rankings are still forming. That's sort of the point of posting: if you've ever wondered whether AI film is developing into anything, come watch a few and leave an honest verdict. Curious what HN thinks about the anti-brigading, "let's see where this is going" ethos.

--help -vvvvvvv

Suggestions? I have a very narrow taste of movies/tv - if someone isn't trying to solve a murder, theft or some locked-room hijinks, I generally can't pay attention to it, so I tend to rewatch Columbo, Banacek and The Rockford Files, but I am liking some of these movies, I love watching the tech but I need people with different tastes and likes.

Let's see how the ai movies continue to grow.

"is this stuff actually getting good, and which models are doing it?". Hot or slop.

My personal interest in ai video, probably stupid - try to actually visualize my dreams through prompts. I've tried it, but it never quite works, but it's fun.

--details

The site doesn't host video (everything plays via youtube-nocookie embeds). The product is the ranking, the many detailed breakdowns of voice sync, glitches, discussions.

If you love looking at coherence and how models are moving along, while seeing short and long form film content that is posted for ai festivals, check it out. Some of them have surprised me a lot. There's some 2 minute short films in here that are legit memorable and make you think, the stuff you imagine has been "let our of people's minds" by these tools.

- Every film records what it was made with (Seedance, Veo, Kling, Sora, mocap, Blender, real footage…), so there are per-tool leaderboards: which models produce watchable film (barren as heckfire right now, use the bookmarklet to add and review? get creators to share more about process)

- Votes only count toward the score if you actually watched a meaningful chunk (tracked via the IFrame API). Verdicts use a Wilson lower bound over reputation-weighted votes, star scores are Bayesian-shrunk toward the site mean, and voter reputation is a Beta distribution updated when a film's verdict settles. An openly pro-AI film site is a brigading magnet from both directions; the math is the defense.

- It tracks AI film festivals as they happen on YouTube i.e. Astana's #SpecialForAAIFF wave, Reply's Venice festival, Chroma, Project Odyssey, each with its verified submissions ranked.

- For the appreciation-society crowd there's a 46-axis breakdown (character consistency, temporal coherence, complex interaction; hands, eating, two bodies, generative necessity, je ne sais quoi). Every axis optional; unrated means not-applicable, not zero.

(I initially added a few to make it 42... then realized I needed more, ho hum)

--verbose details

Stack, for the curious: Go + Postgres + HTMX + Mustache, one binary, no SPA, no analytics vendor. Sign-in is Google, reviewers get generated olde-English pen names.

It's early, the catalogue is ~120 films seeded from festival hashtags and the voting community is tiny, so the rankings are still forming. That's sort of the point of posting: if you've ever wondered whether AI film is developing into anything, come watch a few and leave an honest verdict. Curious what HN thinks about the anti-brigading, "let's see where this is going" ethos.

--help -vvvvvvv

Suggestions? I have a very narrow taste of movies/tv - if someone isn't trying to solve a murder, theft or some locked-room hijinks, I generally can't pay attention to it, so I tend to rewatch Columbo, Banacek and The Rockford Files, but I am liking some of these movies, I love watching the tech but I need people with different tastes and likes.

Let's see how the ai movies continue to grow.

I would love to get people's feedback as it has been helping me a lot with my day-to-day work, but I would like to improve this even further and every feedback helps.

story_text.value:
I'm working in e-commerce for more than 15 years, and the OG images are still one of the mos neglected parts of a shop. On a few projects, even fairly simple product specific image improved the conversion from shared traffic, which is what originally led me to work on this problem.

The new free tool is a browser based Open Graph image designer. You can choose a template, customize the content, add an image and download the OG image. It works without an account and manually uploaded images stay in the browser.

There is also an optional checker for people who do not want to start from scratch. It can inspect your page and create an initial image proposal from its content, which you can then open and adjust in the designer.

I would appreciate feedback on the templates and any customization options that feel missing and of course improvements. Thanks.

story_text.value:
Hey HN,

I’ve been using Google Tasks for years.

It’s fast, simple, and lives inside Gmail — which is why I stuck with it.

But at some point it stops working.

Everything turns into one long flat list, and once you use multiple Google accounts, it gets messy fast.

I didn’t want to switch to something heavier like Jira or Asana. I just wanted Google Tasks to handle a bit more complexity.

So I built something for myself on top of it.

The idea is simple: keep Google as the source of truth, but make it easier to actually use day-to-day — mainly around grouping tasks, handling multiple accounts, and having a clearer “today” view.

I’ve been using it as my main workflow for a while now.

Curious if others tried pushing Google Tasks further,or just switched to something else.

link. https://iloworks.com?utm_source=hackernews
